questions.question: Using Euclid's division algorithm, find the HCF of 196 and 38220.
questions.answer: Apply division algorithm: 38220 = 196 × 195 + 0. The remainder is 0 at the first step, so 196 divides 38220 exactly. HCF(196, 38220) = 196.

questions.question: Prove that √5 is an irrational number.
questions.answer: Proof by contradiction. Suppose √5 is rational: √5 = p/q with p, q integers, q ≠ 0, and gcd(p, q) = 1 (lowest form). Squaring: 5 = p²/q² ⇒ p² = 5q². So 5 | p², hence 5 | p (since 5 is prime). Write p = 5k. Then (5k)² = 5q² ⇒ 25k² = 5q² ⇒ q² = 5k² ⇒ 5 | q² ⇒ 5 | q. But then 5 | p AND 5 | q, contradicting gcd(p, q) = 1. Hence √5 is irrational.

questions.question: Find the LCM and HCF of 12, 15, 21 by the prime-factorisation method. Hence verify that HCF × LCM × (product of remaining factors) is consistent with the product of the three numbers.
questions.answer:
Prime factorisations:
  12 = 2² × 3
  15 = 3 × 5
  21 = 3 × 7

HCF: take the smallest power of each common prime. The only prime common to all three is 3 (exponent 1). HCF = 3.

LCM: take the highest power of each prime appearing in any factorisation. Primes involved: 2, 3, 5, 7. LCM = 2² × 3 × 5 × 7 = 4 × 105 = 420.

Verification: Product of numbers = 12 × 15 × 21 = 3780. HCF × LCM = 3 × 420 = 1260. The two-number identity 'product = HCF × LCM' applies only to two numbers; for three or more it doesn't directly hold. Here 3780 = 1260 × 3, which reflects how the gcd-of-three interacts with pairwise gcds — a useful consistency check but not an identity.
